notes.key_messages:  Candidates must carefully read questions to identify both the type of business and whom they are writing their response about. This will ensure responses are appropriate for each given situation. Information contained in the stem of each question will prove helpful in answering the questions set.  Parts (a) and (b) of each question required the recall of knowledge or application of knowledge linked to a given context. These parts were generally done well. More precision is needed when using business terminology.  Parts (c) and (d) require candidates to identify and explain points. To gain full marks each point must be clearly developed and linked to the relevant context.  Part (e) requires candidates to include more developed explanations and a logical decision based on points made. Candidates should be encouraged to develop, rather than simply list a number of points, and when possible, make a two-sided argument.
notes.general_comments: There was evidence that some candidates did not understand certain parts of the syllabus; having difficulty with concepts such as exchange rates, added value and social enterprise. The application and analysis marks were often not awarded. Some answers given did not constitute an explanation of a point identified, with candidates simply making further points or making a repetition of their initial point. Other candidates did not read the question carefully and so did not address the specific question asked. Candidates must try to use the stimulus information provided to link their answer to the business in question. Candidates should avoid using the same application and analysis point more than once in any given answer. Part (e) of all questions continues to be the most challenging for all candidates. Only the best responses suggested and justified decisions successfully. Others often provided a simple list of knowledge points. Of those who did attempt an evaluative statement, many were unable to provide reasoned statements to back up their choice.
notes.1a: Most candidates understood that the private sector is ‘not government owned.’ Better candidates were able to give a precise definition.
notes.1b: Many candidates understood that redundancy involved losing a job. Some candidates were able to give a precise definition. A common error was to confuse the term with dismissal.
notes.1c: This question proved challenging for most candidates. Those that did well knew that an appreciation would lead to cheaper imports and/or more expensive exports. Application was limited or not attempted in most responses. A common mistake was to confuse exchange rates with tariffs or taxes.
notes.1d: Most candidates were able to identify two ways. Many candidates were able to develop the points to show how they would affect the business. Some did well as they were able to link their answer to the mining business. Instead of development, weaker responses just repeated the knowledge point or simply repeated that it would affect UDig.
notes.1e: This question proved to be a good discriminator. Good knowledge was evident in most responses. The best answers considered points both for and against government help, and then tried to make an appropriate decision based on their argument. These candidates made good use of the source material to support the points being made. Instead of development, weaker answers were characterised by simple statements such as ‘it would protect jobs’. Evaluation in most responses was simple or not attempted.
notes.2a: Most candidates understood that a mass market involved a large number of sales and/or it was for a standard product. Better candidates were able to give a precise definition. A common mistake was to replace the word ‘mass’ with very large which did not explain the term.
notes.2b: This question was generally well answered by most candidates.
notes.2c: Many candidates could identify at least one relevant limitation. Candidates who did well were then able to explain how points such as ‘small sample size’ might be an issue for this beauty business. There were two common errors; firstly, some candidates incorrectly assumed that the market research only consisted of two questions, so identified additional questions that could be included. Secondly, a number of candidates identified only general disadvantages of market research that did not answer the question set.
notes.2d: Relevant advantages were identified by most candidates with points such as attract passing customers and research showing this to be popular way of buying being common choices. Stronger answers made good use of the numbers to help develop these points in context. Weaker answers were characterised by two common mistakes. Instead of development some repeated the knowledge point or explained how the advantage arose rather than how it was could be beneficial. A small number of candidates had the wrong focus, answering the question from the viewpoint of customers.
notes.2e: Good knowledge was evident in most responses. The best responses considered points both for and against each strategy and made an appropriate decision based on the arguments made. These candidates made good use of information from the material provided to support the points being made. Instead of development, weaker answers were characterised by simple statements such as ‘this would increase sales’, without explaining how or why this might be the case. Evaluation in most responses was simple or not attempted.
notes.3a: Many candidates did not understand this term and only the most able scored both marks. There were two common mistakes; repeating the words used in the question or simply identifying ways a business could add value.
notes.3b: This term was not well understood by most candidates and many provided an imprecise definition. Many responses associated it with the costs of selling a product rather than the money spent on producing all the items sold.
notes.3c: This question was well attempted by most candidates. Most responses identified at least one way, with increasing prices and increasing the number of customers being typical examples. The best responses then linked answers to the scenario. A common mistake was to identify ways to increase profits, which was not the question set.
notes.3d: Well answered. Most candidates were able to identify at least one way and were able to explain how points such as loss of customers might create a problem for the restaurant. There were two common mistakes; in some responses, the same point was repeated for both ways while others used the same development. In both instances, the answer could only be credited once.
notes.3e: This question produced a mixture of responses. Good knowledge was evident in many answers. The best responses used the data well to support the points made. Weaker answers were characterised by simple statements such as ‘net profit had increased’. These candidates were not able to develop the points to show how or why such points might be important in deciding whether the business should be pleased with its financial performance. Evaluation in many responses was simple or not attempted.
notes.4a: It was clear that many candidates were not familiar with the term. Many understood that it had objectives other than profit or identified what these other objectives might include. Only the strongest answers were able to give a precise definition.
notes.4c: Most candidates could identify at least one stakeholder group. Candidates who did well were then able to explain why stakeholder groups such as ‘banks’ and ‘the local community’ might be interested in this business. Application in many responses was limited or not attempted.
notes.4d: Most candidates were able to identify one factor with low revenue being the typical issue. Better responses attempted to explain why each factor needed to be considered. Only the best responses linked their answer to the scenario. Instead of development, weaker responses just repeated the knowledge point or simply offered the same explanation for both reasons.
notes.4e: Good knowledge of methods was evident in most responses. Better responses developed the points made and also used the information from the stem to help support the final decision made. Weaker answers listed different methods rather than explain how these methods might be appropriate. Evaluation in most responses was simple or not attempted. BUSINESS STUDIES
